title: Principal human cast
description: Core named and major unnamed human roles; appearances and protagonist blade are game proposals.
prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept. Create original concept art for CINDER Act 2, a game adaptation of H. G. Wells's 1898 The War of the Worlds. Source faithful late-Victorian England, Surrey and London, with alien mechanical terror and invasive red weed. The art direction is independent of Act 1: rust red, charcoal black, warm pale ash, oxidized grey metals; tactile ink-and-gouache concept design with crisp silhouette studies. No lunar theatrical scenery. Human faces and specific costume colors are proposed interpretations where the novel does not specify them. No modern cars, firearms, soldiers, spacecraft, skyscrapers, fantasy armor, mechs with two legs, UFOs, joystick, HUD, watermarks or logos. Each sheet is a finished rich professional development board with generous separation between studies, clear short headings, readable full-body silhouettes, material swatches and close-ups. Eight full-body character design studies: unnamed philosophical narrator in a worn dark frock coat and waistcoat; his wife with travel cloak and practical late-Victorian dress; youthful medical-student brother; Ogilvy the astronomer with tweed jacket and field notebook; Henderson the journalist with period hat and notebook; Stent the Astronomer Royal with formal dark suit; pale distressed curate in black clerical dress; exhausted artilleryman in late-1890s British field uniform, red accents muted. Distinct readable bodies and expressions. Lower strip shows narrator front/back/dash silhouette with one short blade, only as a game protagonist adaptation. Human NPCs remain human and civilian-friendly, not enemy bosses. Cream presentation board, rust-black accents. Label each name/role.
notes: Original generated game concept; not an archival image, production asset, or implemented level. Details and layouts are proposals. Decorative text and any quotation-like captions on generated boards are unverified graphic embellishments, not quotations from Wells.
